utterances.text: And this ad hoc hospital, sir, was actually operating out of a church which had big red crosses placed outside it; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: It was a church, or it had been a church, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you, yourself, see any of the red crosses placed outside of the church to alert people it was a medical [Realtime transcript read in error "military"] facility?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I can't remember that, if it was red cross signed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, you described one conversation that you had had with a gentleman named Franjo Kristo, the predecessor of Mr. Drago Ljubos as the chief of civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Can you tell me when it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it's the bottom of page 3 of your statement. While you are locating that, let me correct an error on the record. Line 15 on page 56 it says "military facility." I think the question was "medical facility." But the question that I want to raise with you, commandant, is the comments that were made to you by Mr. Kristo relating to Muslims, it's not unusual in times of war, so far as you are aware, to talk in disparaging terms about the enemy, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that's a helpful question. We know that from our own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with the mosque fire, sir, that occurred, I believe, on September the 27th, 1993, you have told us that Mr. Maric informed you that there would be an investigation into that fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But he stressed to you that there were numerous Croatian refugees in the town and that it was actually difficult to control the criminal elements within the new refugees, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so you visited the chief of civilian police in Busovaca, Mr. Drago Ljubos, and he actually told you that this incident was, in fact, being investigated; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he also stressed to you that the civilian police had taken all necessary measures to protect the Muslim minority in Busovaca; did he not?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so that was the same message as you were given a few months earlier by the chief of military police, Mr. Milic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to one other incident, sir, the incident involving the two soldiers that shot at you.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You actually noted contemporaneously on October the 2nd that these -- this incident was caused because one of the soldiers was actually in love with one of the people that was being moved out of Vitez municipality, and he wanted to stop that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's what was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the written report that you received, or the written letter that you received from Colonel Blaskic a few days later, confirmed what you, in fact, had written in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I had referred earlier, sir, to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosnia. Let me just ask you, were you at all familiar with the ongoing negotiations and the European community was holding with representatives of the Serbs, Croats and Muslims that ultimately resulted in the Stoltenberg-Owen plan for the governments of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I knew there was negotiations going on, but I can't tell you who was participating and who had the power to speak for his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me suggest to you that one of the -- that the principal document that emerged from the Stoltenberg-Owen plan was called a constitutional agreement of the union of republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that it actually envisaged three constituent republics: One to be a Muslim republic; one to be a Croat; and one to be a Serb republic. Does that ring a bell of familiarity to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And were you aware that the Croats actually founded a Croat republic of -- a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosnia on August the 28th, 1993, shortly after the final version of the Stoltenberg-Owen plan was drafted?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I know, and I remember it was founded, but I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The founding document was actually signed by a gentleman by the name of Perica Jukic. Do you know who that gentleman is or have you never met him?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't recognise the name?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that you yourself never discovered what Mr. Kordic's position or post in this new republic was, if any?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of the -- I just have a few final questions, sir. One of the subjects that you covered was a visit to Busovaca on August the 21st of 1993, where you were introduced to a so-called Mujahedin soldier, a Syrian, by the name of Kemal Muhamed Mustafa. Is it my understanding that this gentlemen told you he had been a student since 1982?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's what he told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he mentioned to you that he had been mobilised. Mobilised by whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: By the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were actually informed by the ABiH forces themselves on September the 4th of 1993, and I think you can find it on page 5 of your statement to refresh your memory, but you were told that the ABiH was in the process of putting together a new Muslim brigade in the Zenica area, and that this would be placed under the command of General Dzemal Merdan; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just a few questions on the subject of helicopters. Let me suggest to you, sir, that Mr. Valenta and Mr. Maric were actually flown down to Neum in United Nations helicopters, having travelled to Kiseljak under the guard of warriors, and that they flew from Kiseljak to Neum. Does that ring a bell, or don't you have any knowledge on that subject?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: This can be possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself, sir, never saw any Croatian army troops in Central Bosnia at any time during your three-month tour, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: What do you mean, Croatian army troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good question. I mean troops from the army of the Republic of Croatia as opposed to troops from the Croat forces in Central Bosnia, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And here are the final questions that I've got for you, commandant. Wouldn't you agree that you encountered an extremely complicated situation when you arrived in Central Bosnia, politically, militarily and ethnically?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, and this is no -- certainly no criticism of you or your ECMM colleagues, but would it be fair to say that you found the military, political and ethnic situation often confused and confusing?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I would say in the same way as the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mean that as far as you are aware, the rest of the world found it confused and confusing too?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's what I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you say, commandant, that it took you three months just to come to grips with a basic understanding of what was confronting you?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, as I told before, it's very delicate, and it was very difficult to understand. There are several reasons. But my mission was to speak with people and to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, commandant, I'm sure that you did your job as well as you could, you discharged your duty conscientiously and effectively. But it's fair to say that you left after this three-month period only to be replaced by other monitors who had to go through the same learning process that you had just gone through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for comment, I think. Anything else, because we need to finish this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Commandant, did you find it frustrating to be shipped out of the area just as you learned enough to start understanding this situation in which you found yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. No need to answer that question. No need to answer that. It's a personal matter. It's not going to help us, what the witness may or may not have felt. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, that concludes my questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Verhoeven, my name is Bozidar Kovacic. I am a lawyer from Zagreb. With my colleague Goran Mikulicic, I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez. I shall speak in Croatian and should also like to ask you to make a pause before answering so that the interpreters can finish their interpretation. Of course, if I am not clear enough in asking my questions, please do tell me so. And let us then resume where my learned friend Sayers left off. When you came to Bosnia, from the point of view of military positions, rather the strategic advantage, was it obvious that in the Vitez area in the Lasva Valley the HVO was at a disadvantage as against the Bosnian -- the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: As a soldier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I believe you will also agree with me that it was an enclave and that, militarily speaking, the important position, sir, that is positions in the hills above the roads and around the roads, were held by Muslim forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the beginning of your testimony today you said that you met Cerkez for the first time on the 31st of July '93, that you believed it was in his office and that you discussed the exchange of prisoners. And in point of fact, Cerkez proposed, and I should say he insisted on an exchange on the basis of an all-for-all principle. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of the briefing, because you were new to the area, did you learn in those briefings that some people were swapped for some people, and that this was the first time that Cerkez insisted on all for all?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: What is "swapped"? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Exchanged. Swapped, exchanged. Well, evidently a misunderstanding. In the exchanges of prisoners until that time, specific individuals were exchanged, and this was the first time that Cerkez proposed to exchange all for all; that is, all prisoners kept by one side for all prisoners kept by the other side?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I don't know if it was the first time; just at that meeting, Mr. Cerkez told -- he wanted an exchange, all for all. I don't know if it was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. And with some exceptions, which you mentioned in relation to those three boys, those prisoners were, in point of fact, prisoners of war; that is, individuals captured during fighting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: As I was told, the boys were not involved with fighting when they were kept. I was told they were working on the field, and they were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the same incident -- that is, the capture of those boys -- did you hear that an elderly man who was working in the field with them was killed on that same occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is quite possible, but did you have an opportunity to hear, because you received information about those boys and visited them -- no, let me rephrase this: Did you talk to those boys directly when you visited them in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did one of them complain that he was used for trench digging, or rather that he was tied with a rope to a tree as he was digging a trench?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I don't think he told this to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter with you when you visited those boys in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, we were always with interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understood how your work was organised, and I should like to clarify certain points. In the area the boundaries of which are roughly Zenica, Guca Gora, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Kruscica, Busovaca, and then back to Travnik, in that area, were there two or three ECMM teams?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: There was one team. It was Victor 1. But we had another team, and that was the humanitarian team, who covered the other areas of the -- the field teams, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Verhoeven, that is an area -- if you go up as far as Guca Gora, and you also went there, this is an area of some 300 kilometres square, to round it off, so surely you couldn't know what happened on a daily basis over such a wide area?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's for sure. It was impossible in one day to do all the area. There were some places where I had never been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let us not waste time with maps. I believe you can confirm to me that Kruscica is to the south of Vitez. It is beyond dispute, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as you crossed the line there, could we agree that immediately before Kruscica, if you use that road from the main road southward, that that was the demarcation line, the line separating the HVO from the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it is natural for the HVO soldiers, as you are coming from their territory to go into Kruscica, it is natural for them to control all the persons passing there; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: There were agreements that ECMM members who were visibly in their cars, dressed in white, with white cars, could pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: True. And on such occasions, you would come to such a checkpoint, and the army had to establish your identity, isn't it, in order to let you pass to the other side?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now I should like to ask you, because you still have with you the document Z1186,2, it is an ECMM daily report of the 27th [as interpreted] of August, '93. Would you please look at page 2 and this passage at the top of the page. You told us already that at this checkpoint, before Kruscica, that you had no authorisations issued by Blaskic in writing, and that is true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I should first correct you, sir; it's not a daily report of the 27th of August but of 30 August.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I did say 30th of August. The interpreter's mistake. I am referring to the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: So about your question, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, the soldiers who were at that demarcation line were members of a brigade, and they asked for permission from their commander; that is, the person directly superior to them. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I can tell you -- I can't tell you. So I can't tell you if those soldiers belonged to which brigade or -- of course, they were not wearing all the same uniforms; they had no signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But be that as it may, according to this information, it transpires that you asked for permission from Cerkez, and that you were told on that occasion that he would have given it to you anyway, but the only question that was raised was the question of your safety, because they believed that an offensive action might take place at any moment; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does it mean anything to you when I say -- when I try to remind you that, in fact, a very forceful offensive of the BH army in that area, not far from Kruscica, started that day? It was near a village called Bobasi. Does this jog your memory? They are not mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: By memory, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And since we are looking at this document, under Item 8, we here have an ECMM assessment, and it talks about different currents within the BH army, if I may call it that. This refers to strangers and to local Muslims. Did you, before that or after that, come across that particular problem; that is, foreigners who were called hardliners, and local Muslims whose approach was different in relation to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes. This problem was even also said by some Muslim commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, and I believe it was roughly at the same time, you said that Cerkez expected an attack of the BH army, and that everything that had happened until then had been a game? I am referring to the end of August 1993, so that period of time. Is it true that after that forceful BiH army offensive ensued and that the war became a much more -- a much graver, a much more serious affair than at the time when you arrived in the territory?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I don't know if -- because I wasn't there, if it was worse or not before. But it's true that both sides tried to get the over hand on the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I think that you will agree in connection with what we said at the outset that the BiH Army had the initiative and that it had better strategic positions as compared to the HVO in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at that time the BiH Army had 10 to 12.000 soldiers who were permanently stationed in this zone, in this operative zone in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many it were, but it's obviously, when you look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which map are you referring to? Do you have a map with the actual strength of the forces concerned marked on that map? We haven't got that kind of a map.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. I meant when you look at the enclave from the Croat community. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at your report for the 31st of August 1993. It is Z1187,1. On page 2 there is a section above the words listed under number 4, above "humanitarian activity." There is a comment of yours here saying that Blaskic had certain problems with Mario Cerkez, the commander of the brigade. Was this specifically stated to you? Was it because he could not keep the front line and thus carry out his assignment during the BiH Army offensive? Is that the problem, or was it perhaps something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: This was told to me by the liaison officer of the HVO, and if my memories are well, it was a problem of communication between those two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are not in a position to state this more specifically, except that you can say a problem of communication?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: This is what the liaison officer told to me. I have never seen both men arguing or having a fight, if it is that what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In this same report, a few lines up in this same paragraph, again reference is made to Kruscica and the checkpoint, and it also says that the local commander said that it was too dangerous to go towards Kruscica because of sniper activity or, rather, that he could not de-mine the road because of sniper activity coming from the Bosnian side. Do you remember these events?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is correct that there was sniper activity from the other side? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Do you mean if I have been shot at at the moment when I was at the checkpoint or what do you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I am not referring to you personally, but you saw at that checkpoint that while you were talking the BiH Army was firing up from the hills.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, it happened. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It happened. All right. And finally -- no, I am sorry. I apologise. I am going to leave that. Mr. Verhoeven, tell me, please, did you ever see or hear about Cerkez appearing in any other place except for Vitez or the immediate vicinity of Vitez, like Busovaca, Novi Travnik or any other place in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us be quite clear on this. To the best of your knowledge, at the time when you were there, Cerkez was a local commander in the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That is the way I knew it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report dated the 20th of September 1993, number Z1207,1, once again there is information about Kruscica and information to the effect that over 100 shells had been fired in the zone of Vitez; and that the HVO took part of the area that it had lost in Kruscica, the front line in Kruscica or, rather, that it had remained the same after all. And then a bit lower -- I mean, we don't really have to read all of this, mention is made -- I'm sorry. It is said that 50 civilians were wounded and 12 killed; that soldiers are not included in this figure; and that the HVO does not have information concerning the exact number as far as military casualties are concerned. Not to mention all the other information that we have, but based on this picture, do we agree that during those days, that is to say around the 20th of September, the BiH Army obviously was on the offensive, as far as Vitez is concerned, and was obviously predominant in this situation when such a large number of civilians even got killed, and the military part of the HVO doesn't even know it's own number of casualties exactly. So is that a correct picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I observe, that's a very long question, almost impossible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Incomprehensible. What is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I can rephrase it. The question is: Isn't it clear, on the basis of this information, that the dominant force was the BiH Army; that it had military initiative totally, and that is why there was such a large number of civilian casualties and the number of military casualties is not even known? Do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: First of all, when you speak about the number of casualties, these are informations given by the HVO liaison officer, as I put in my report. He said about the shelling, about 20 rounds in 10 minutes. That is what I saw. So the number of casualties, I can't -- I couldn't control this. This is what was told by the liaison officer of the HVO. Now, the second part of your question, that the BiH Army was in a better position at that moment, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your interlocutor from the HVO told you that while these events were actually taking place; is that right? This was up-to-date information? He was not talking about weeks, previous weeks, he was talking about the present day? It was a question of yesterday, today, tomorrow, so it was very up-to-date, is that right? And that was Darko Gelic, if I am not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct. He talked about the 19th of September, early in the morning, as I put it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, until then Darko Gelic was always as good as his word; whatever he told you proved to be true and correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: It is difficult to find proofs on matters of wounded and killed people, so reported what they said, and so we did on both sides. Like in all wars, I think that every part will, perhaps, give a little bit more of own casualties to be able to complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite understandable. However, tell me, you communicated quite often with Darko Gelic, didn't you? Not only you personally, but your other colleagues as well, and you believed him to be a credible person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, that I haven't been able to really prove that he was not credible or that he lied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As for the threat that you heard about, the HVO threat, that they would blow up the explosives factory, because they had no other way out, could you please look at your document, your report from the 27th of September. That is 1217,1. The last two lines on page 1. Could you please have a look at them. It has to do with your conversation with Mr. Beba, who was deputy commander of the BiH Army in Travnik. And he assured you that this threat was a mere bluff; that the explosives factory would be blown up. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact words, but as I wrote it down at that very moment, he will have said it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you recall today what your own assessment was, whether it was a bluff, or did the HVO really want to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you don't know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: This is a -- this is a very difficult -- I know I was very worried at that moment, and I spoke to several people. It was a second time said by -- I don't get the name any more -- that they would do it. I can't tell you if it was a bluff or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would also like to draw your attention to your report dated the 23rd of September, 1993. That is number 1212,1. You mentioned this during your earlier testimony, that shells fell near the place where you were talking to Gelic, but this was a sequel to the offensive that had started a few days earlier and that was also taken note of in your reports. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just two or three questions more related to the incident when your vehicle was shot at and when you went to complain to Blaskic. That was an ad hoc meeting, wasn't it? You came there and you asked for a meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: It was not really a predated meeting. The car was broke down; we just managed to get to the -- to Vitez headquarters, and I immediately -- I exist -- no, I assist -- assist? How you call?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You insist?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I insist, correct, yeah. I insist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic -- I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Verhoeven. Look, we've got to terminate very quickly. Is there any other point -- I think we have the point about the meeting. Is there any point you want to make, or are we going to have to go into tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this, I only have one more question left, which is going to take half a minute. And after that, I do have a few more questions; not very many, but I believe I have about ten minutes left, or so, those that were not touched upon in the previous cross-examination. In relation to this particular event, only one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, we really didn't understand -- you want these minutes for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one more question on the subject that we've been discussing so far, so I need only ten more seconds for that. And then after that, I have a few other questions. One is rather closely related to Cerkez; one is related to the area of Vitez, in a narrower sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, we'll give you five more minutes to finish with this witness. You've got to arrange it so that you can finish in five minutes, because this witness mustn't come back tomorrow for five minutes. Finish what you have to do, please, in the next five minutes; otherwise we are going to put an end to it and ask Mr. Nice to end his examination as well, because we've got a hearing for another case this afternoon. Please finish within the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really going to do away with everything which I believe is not absolutely essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Verhoeven, what we discussed was on the 2nd of October, of 1993, that incident. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And actually, Cerkez just happened to be there, because your conversation with Blaskic took place in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he did not take part in the conversation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: This, I don't remember any more, who said what. I was just shut out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In connection with that, you received a letter from Blaskic which we saw; did you ever find out anything about this, which units the persons mentioned in that letter belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know that at least this first person, Medjugorac, was a member of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he did not know. If he did not know, he didn't. There's no point going on. Now, are there any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This list of names that you produced, Z1218, I would just like to draw your attention to the last name on the first page, under number 3, Vitez HVO. I'm not sure I can read this well. That is the chief of the civilian police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of meeting this person?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this section entitled "Vitez," that is to say, persons from Vitez, Cerkez is mentioned last, and it says here, "Commander of the Viteska Brigade." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the HVO side, a woman is also mentioned, Evica Saric; and according to this description, she is chairman of the commission for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's the way she was presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was she a civilian, or a member of the military segment of the HVO? How was she introduced?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: She was introduced as president of the commission of the prisoners of war. But it was at that moment very difficult to know if someone was a soldier or someone was a civilian, because civilians were carrying arms and soldiers, armed soldiers, were carrying civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just one more question in relation to the no-fly zone. You will agree that at that time in Bosnia there was a no-fly zone; there was a total ban on flights. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Every side had to announce each and every flight and receive permission for it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, because it was a no-fly zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And these permits were issued by UNPROFOR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, please ask your question. Ask your last question. What is this about? What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It stems from that that every flight had to be announced to UNPROFOR; otherwise, it would have been a free target. Any unit could shoot down such a plane, was entitled to do that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I know it was a no-fly zone, but I don't know how the procedures were to get permission for flight. I didn't belong to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My last, final question related to this. UNPROFOR gave permission for medical flights; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He is not a member of UNPROFOR. Concentrate, please, on asking relevant questions which the witness can answer. Now, have you any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that it was reasonable to expect that this witness and his people could have had such information, but of course I'm not going to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing: The waterworks in the area of Vitez, did you ever go to the water station above Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I think that the cross-examination is now complete -- I'm speaking for my colleague here -- as you were told you were given five minutes; it's now been ten minutes. In addition, the question has nothing to do with the direct examination. I think we can now give Mr. Nice the floor if he has anything he wants to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three questions capable of yes/no answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the helicopter you saw bear United Nations insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did anyone, including the Bosnians you were speaking to, but did anyone ever talk of the United Nations flying people to their parliament in Neum?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you visited the three boys in prison, detained, rather, did you visit them alone, or with anyone else? If so, whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: The entire team, I think there were, but they didn't get into the place where the boys were. They stayed outside, the guardians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the team would include Watkins and others, would it?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: No, I should have to look at the testimony, who was with me, because I did not drive all the time with Bekos or Watkins. It changed, also; the team was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we'll find the team. There is one last question. You were asked questions about the nature of the chain of command and comparing it with ordinary military forces. Were you ever actually given detailed information, of the nature of who commanded whom, like who commanded the military police, or did you have to try and work this out for yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHAN VERHOEVEN
utterances.text: I did have to work it out myself by questioning people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Verhoeven, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded and you are free to go. Let me add this. That although Mr. Kovacic has received most of the criticism today for the amount of time that's been taken out, it would be more just if it was spread equally between all the parties. I would ask everybody to concentrate on deciding what is relevant and trying to cut out this enormous amount of detail which is taking up time, is inconveniencing witnesses and inconveniencing the Trial Chamber. And that applies to all sides, not just to Mr. Kovacic. Yes, tomorrow morning, 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1.14 p.m. to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of November, 1999.
